summary: Updates RFC 5280 by replacing the X.509 policy validation algorithm with an equivalent, more efficient one. The original built a structure that could grow exponentially in the worst case, leaving implementations open to denial-of-service attacks.

eli5.summary: An old checklist could balloon so big that a computer got stuck. This swaps it for a faster list giving the same answers.

questions: what is the x509 policy graph
subtitle: A fix for X.509 policy validation that stops a small certificate chain from blowing up a validator's memory and time.

tldr.problem: The policy validation algorithm in RFC 5280 builds a policy tree that can grow exponentially with the length of a certification path, so a small attacker-supplied chain can cost a validator far more than it costs to send.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9618 replaces the tree with a policy graph in which duplicate nodes are merged into one node with several parents. The graph grows linearly and gives the same validity results and the same valid policies.
tldr.outcome: Implementations SHOULD use the graph and SHOULD NOT output the full valid_policy_tree. RFC 9618 updates RFC 5280 and also lists other mitigations for implementations that cannot switch.

today: RFC 9618 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2024 that updates RFC 5280. It has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: How X.509 Policy Validation Works
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines extensions for working out which policies apply to a certification path. A policy is described by an object identifier (OID) and a set of optional qualifiers. The certificate policies extension lists the policies under which a certificate was issued. The policy mappings extension lets a CA certificate map its policy OIDs to other policy OIDs in certificates it issues. The path's overall policy set is the intersection of the policies asserted by each certificate in the path.

Section 6.1 of RFC 5280 computes this set during path validation by building a policy tree of the policies asserted by each certificate and the mappings between them. RFC 9618 states that this tree can grow exponentially in the depth of the path.
sections.eli5: Each certificate in a chain says which rules it follows, and some can say "my rule A counts as your rule B". The validator keeps a family tree of these rules to see which ones hold the whole way along.

sections.title: The Denial-of-Service Problem
sections.content:
In the RFC 5280 algorithm a node's parent is the issuer policy that was mapped to it, and its children are the policies it was mapped to in the subject certificate. A single policy P can produce multiple child nodes if multiple issuer policies map to P, and that makes the tree grow multiplicatively at each level.

The RFC's example is a chain where every intermediate certificate asserts OID1 and OID2 and contains all four mappings between them (OID1 to OID1, OID1 to OID2, OID2 to OID1, OID2 to OID2). At each depth the tree doubles in size.

An attacker sends such a chain and triggers certificate validation, for example against a TLS server that validates client certificates. The target spends far more resources than the attacker did, which stops it from serving other clients. The RFC cites CVE-2023-0464 and CVE-2023-23524 as examples of this vulnerability.
sections.eli5: Imagine every time you copy a sticker, each copy asks for two more copies. After a few rounds you have a mountain of stickers, though you only asked for one. A tiny letter from an attacker can make the computer do that.

sections.title: From Policy Tree to Policy Graph
sections.content:
The tree is wasteful because when several issuer policies map to one subject policy, that policy appears as several duplicate nodes, and its children are then duplicated recursively. A policy graph is a directed acyclic graph that stores each policy once, as a single node with multiple parents.

The graph's size is bounded linearly by the total number of certificate policies and policy mappings. The old tree is the set of all paths from the root to a leaf in the graph, so no information is lost.

X.509 implementations SHOULD validate policy by building the graph. The one visible difference is in the output. Section 6.1.6 of RFC 5280 returned the whole valid_policy_tree, but ITU-T X.509 only describes the authorities-constrained policies, the user-constrained policies and their qualifiers as outputs. Implementations SHOULD NOT output the whole tree, and MAY omit policy qualifiers.
sections.eli5: Instead of drawing the same box again and again, you draw it once and point several arrows at it. The picture stays small and tells the same story.

sections.title: The Replacement Text for RFC 5280
sections.content:
Section 5 gives exact replacement text for parts of RFC 5280 Section 6.1.

  • The state variable becomes valid_policy_graph. Each node holds a valid policy, a set of qualifiers and an expected policy set. At most one node per depth has a given policy OID. A node cannot be a child of both anyPolicy and some other OID.
  • Steps (d), (e) and (f) of Section 6.1.3 are rewritten to add child nodes with possibly several parents, handle anyPolicy, and prune nodes that have no children.
  • Step (b) of Section 6.1.4 is rewritten for policy mappings.
  • Step (g) of Section 6.1.5 computes the user-constrained policy set from the graph.
  • Section 6.1.6 now returns the user-constrained policy set and the working public key data. Computing the old valid_policy_tree is deprecated and NOT RECOMMENDED. A legacy system that needs it may build it from the graph by duplicating every multi-parent node, but that may take exponential time and memory, so such implementations SHOULD limit tree depth or size.

The document states that the change does not alter the validity of any path or which policies are valid for it.
sections.eli5: This part is the exact rewrite of the old rulebook pages, so that people building certificate checkers can follow the new method step by step.

sections.title: Other Mitigations
sections.content:
Implementations that cannot move to the graph SHOULD mitigate the attack in other ways. The RFC lists five.

  • Verify signatures first. Validators SHOULD check signatures before or together with policy checks. This limits the attack to those who control CA certificates, which may not be enough for applications that evaluate an untrusted PKI.
  • Limit certificate depth. This may reject real paths if set too low, and may still allow attacks if set too high.
  • Limit policy tree size. Reject the path when the limit is reached.
  • Inhibit policy mapping through initial-policy-mapping-inhibit. It breaks paths that rely on mapping, so CAs SHOULD NOT issue certificates with the policy mappings extension.
  • Disable policy checking. Critical policy-related extensions such as policy constraints MUST then be treated as unrecognized and rejected.
sections.eli5: If you cannot switch to the new checklist, you can still stay safe by checking the signatures first, setting a size limit, or skipping the rule-copying feature.
